newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Women overlooked in Romanian presidential race.
newsitem.headline: Women overlooked in Romanian presidential race.

text.p: Romania's presidential election may be a watershed in the country's post-communist development but it has overlooked those probably worst affected by the tumultuous changes since 1989 -- women.
Neither ex-communist incumbent Ion Iliescu nor centrist foe Emil Constantinescu have devoted much of a torrid campaign to what people in the West would regard as women's issues.
Discussion has been limited to increasing family allowances, extending maternity leave and offering young couples credits to buy their homes.
"The male candidates have relied solely on their charm to capture women's votes," said Daniela Crasnaru, a poet and one of Romania's rare female politicians.
"All other social groups were either lured with promises by various parties or at least flattered. But not women."

In parliamentary elections this month, only 25 of 486 seats contested were won by women. One of the winners was Romania's sole female cabinet minister in the outgoing government -- appointed to the health portfolio in August.

Chauvinist attitudes in Romania have relegated women to subservient roles at home, in the workplace and particularly in politics. Feminist attitudes are rare, lobbies non-existent. Legal protection afforded women under late communist dictator Nicolae Ceausescu has disappeared.
There is no talk of a role for the future "first lady" after Sunday's vote.
Politicians keep their spouses well out of view -- mindful of how Ceausescu's wife Elena struck fear into politicians and revulsion in the public for her overbearing role in government.
Iliescu appears in public with his engineer wife Nina only when voting at his local polling station.

He told a television talk show hostess that his wife ran the family budget. But when U.S. First Lady Hillary Clinton visited Bucharest in July, Nina was nowhere to be seen -- the foreign minister's wife was drafted in to escort her instead.
Constantinescu's wife Nadia, a lawyer, has said she respects his wish she not have a prominent role if he won.

"Like many men, my husband wants what he calls a Japanese wife, quiet, always smiling, patient and accommodating," she said. "I have not been involved in my husband's public activities and will not do so. I don't want to give up my job."
Women at the other end of the scale have borne the brunt of the transition to a market economy. They are invariably the first victims of poverty and unemployment.
Dwindling health care budgets hit ante and post-natal care and infant mortality rates remain among the highest in Europe.
Abortion, banned under Ceausescu's drive for population increase, remains the main form of contraception, though it has halved from a 1990 peak of one million.
Although some women are beating the odds by making strides in the media and fledgling post-communist businesses, politics is likely to remain a closed shop to them for some time.

"In politics, women are Scheherazades who have to save their heads every day by telling their sultans another new and wonderful story," Crasnaru said, referring to the heroine of the Arabian Nights story cycle.
